assessment_strategy.1. Verify Article 10 Applicability and A: First, identify the exact expression or expressive conduct at issue and decide whether it falls within Article 10’s broad scope: speech, writing, art, photographs, satire, commercial speech, political speech, online activity, journalistic work, whistleblowing, private correspondence, witness statements, or expressive conduct. Also consider special Article 10 contexts such as access to State-held information, source protection, Internet use, or labour-related speech. Exclude only material clearly outside protection, such as expression removed by Article 17 or statements whose sole purpose is wanton insult. Then check the usual admissibility filters: exhaustion of domestic remedies, victim status, and whether the applicant suffered a significant disadvantage. In access-to-information cases, verify the four threshold elements: the request’s purpose, the public-interest nature of the information, the requester’s role as a public watchdog or equivalent, and whether the information was ready and available. If Article 10 is inapplicable or the application is inadmissible, stop; otherwise proceed to the next step.

assessment_strategy.2. Determine Whether There Was an Interf: Next, define the impugned State act or omission and assess its real effects rather than its domestic legal label. Decide whether there was an interference with freedom of expression, or, in a positive-obligation case, whether the State failed to secure the practical and effective exercise of that freedom. Relevant interferences include criminal, civil, disciplinary or employment sanctions; dismissal or refusal to appoint; investigations or detention with a chilling effect; seizure, confiscation or destruction of material; publication bans; refusal of access to information or places; disclosure orders against journalists; blocking websites or online content; licensing refusals; or penalties for social-media activity. Pay particular attention to chilling effects, including warnings, stayed proceedings, acquittals reached only after lengthy prosecution, or sanctions likely to deter future speech. If you find no interference and no failure of positive protection, predict no violation of Article 10 and stop; otherwise proceed.

assessment_strategy.3. Test the Justification: Was the Measu: Then assess whether the interference had a basis in domestic law and whether that law met the Convention’s quality requirements: accessibility, foreseeability, and sufficient safeguards against arbitrary or abusive use. The Court generally defers to domestic interpretation unless it is arbitrary or manifestly unreasonable, but it must still verify that vague concepts, criminal provisions, online-liability rules, confidentiality rules, or licensing powers were applied in a sufficiently precise and predictable manner. If the measure was not prescribed by law, predict a violation and skip the next step. If it was lawful, identify the legitimate aim relied on and verify that it is one of the exhaustive aims in Article 10 § 2: national security, territorial integrity, public safety, prevention of disorder or crime, protection of health or morals, protection of the reputation or rights of others, prevention of disclosure of confidential information, or maintenance of the authority and impartiality of the judiciary. If no genuine legitimate aim is established, predict a violation and stop; otherwise proceed.

assessment_strategy.4. Assess Necessity in a Democratic Soci: Finally, decide whether the interference answered a pressing social need and was proportionate to the legitimate aim pursued. Review whether the domestic courts gave relevant and sufficient reasons and applied Strasbourg standards; if they did, depart from their assessment only for strong reasons, but if they did not, conduct your own balancing or find a violation. In all cases assess: (a) the contribution of the expression to a debate of public interest; (b) the status of the speaker (journalist, NGO, politician, lawyer, judge, whistleblower, academic, company, private individual) and whether enhanced protection applies; (c) the status of the target (public figure, public authority, judge, prosecutor, company, private person, vulnerable group); (d) the content, form, tone, and context of the speech, including satire, artistic expression, incitement, hate speech, separatist or terrorist context, or impact on minors or vulnerable persons; (e) the distinction between facts and value judgments, the existence of a sufficient factual basis, good faith, and responsible journalism; (f) the method of obtaining information, its veracity, confidentiality, and, where relevant, source protection; and (g) the nature and severity of the sanction, including whether a less restrictive measure was available, whether a criminal conviction itself had a chilling effect, and whether damages, injunctions, dismissal, detention, licence revocation, or blocking orders were excessive. Where Article 10 conflicts with another Convention right, especially Articles 8, 6 § 2, 9, or 11, perform a fair-balance analysis using the Court’s context-specific criteria: public interest, notoriety, prior conduct, content and consequences of publication, method of obtaining information, seriousness of reputational harm, and effect on proceedings or private life. If the State’s reasons are insufficient, the balance is defective, or the sanction is disproportionate, predict a violation; otherwise predict no violation.
